leads.text:
38 E. 64th St., LLC v Nile, Inc. 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06881 
 November 19, 2026 
 Appellate Division, First Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 38 East 64th Street, LLC, Plaintiff-Appellant, 
 v 
 Nile, Inc. et al., Defendants-Respondents, XYZ Corp. et al., Defendants. 

 Decided and Entered: November 19, 2026 
 Index No. 650912/24|Appeal No. 7544|Case No. 2025-04212| 
 Before: Webber, J.P., Kapnick, Pitt-Burke, Chan, Parker-Raso, JJ. 

 Belkin Burden Goldman, LLP, New York (Mark N. Antar of counsel), for appellant. 
 David Rozenholc & Associates, New York (James B. Fishman of counsel), for respondents. 

 [*1] 
 Order, Supreme Court, New York County (Lyle E. Frank, J.), entered May 19, 2025, which denied plaintiff's motion under CPLR 3212 for summary judgment in its favor on its complaint and dismissal of defendants' counterclaims, and under CPLR 3211 for dismissal of defendants' affirmative defenses, unanimously affirmed, without costs. 
 In this action, plaintiff sought to recover possession and use and occupancy of the apartment rented to defendant Nile, Inc., a company owned by defendant E. Terese Carpenter, beginning in and around 2006. Plaintiff also sought attorneys' fees in accordance with the lease. 
 Under the circumstances presented, Supreme Court correctly denied plaintiff's motion. We have held for rent stabilization code purposes, where "there is a question of fact concerning whether the premises at issue are being used for mixed residential and commercial use, that question must be resolved in the first instance by the factfinder" ( Hadzovic v Buckley Sch. in the City of N.Y. , 238 AD3d 487 , 489 [1st Dept 2026]). 
 Defendants submitted evidence sufficient to raise an issue of fact as to whether the unit was used for residential purposes with the landlord's knowledge and acquiescence, thus implicating the rent stabilization regulations ( see Glebow Realty Assoc. v Dietrich , 227 AD3d 610 , 611 [1st Dept 2024]). Plaintiff does not dispute defendants' assertions that it required them to enter into a commercial lease exclusively for business use of an apartment previously subject to the rent stabilization law even though the building's certificate of occupancy permitted only residential use. Moreover, plaintiff failed to provide evidence disputing defendants' assertion that Carpenter, Nile's principal, always intended to reside, and did in fact reside, in the apartment for over 20 years ( see Matter of 20 W. 76th St. v Division of Hous. & Community Renewal , 306 AD2d 6, 7-8 [1st Dept 2003]). 
 Further, defendants stated a cause of action with respect to both their counterclaims. Defendants sufficiently alleged that Carpenter's occupancy is subject to the Rent Stabilization Law and that plaintiff illegally and fraudulently deregulated the unit, if proven would entitle Carpenter to a judgment declaring that she is the lawful rent-stabilized tenant of the unit. 
 We have considered plaintiff's remaining arguments and find them unavailing. 
 THIS CONSTITUTES THE DECISION AND ORDER OF THE SUPREME COURT, APPELLATE DIVISION, FIRST DEPARTMENT. 
 ENTERED: November 19, 2026

Appellee Wilmington Savings Fund Society, F .S.B. 
David E. Wilks, Esquire, WILKS LAW, LLC, Wilmington, Delaware, Attorney for 
Appellants H. Adam Wahl, III, and Brookside Properties, LLC.  
LUGG, J. 
2 
 
INTRODUCTION 
Quality HV AC borrowed $6,000,000.00 from WSFS.  H. Adam Wahl, III 
(“Wahl”) and Brookside Properties (“Brookside”) guaranteed the loan.  Quality 
HV AC defaulted, and WSFS moved to secure its financial interest.  WSFS invoked 
provisions of the guarantees to seek confessions of judgment against the loan 
guarantors – Wahl and Brookside.  The guarantors opposed.  They contend WSFS 
failed to demonstrate the guarantors knowingly, intelligently, and voluntarily waived 
their due process rights.   
A Superior Court Commissioner  concluded that Wahl knowingly, 
intentionally, and voluntarily waived , on behalf of himself and Brookside, the 
guarantors’ rights to notice and a hearing .1  Wahl appealed the Commissioner’s 
findings. 2  
 
1 Wahl I, 2025 WL 2206759; Wahl II, 2026 WL 1747746. 
2 Defendants appealed the Superior Court Commissioner’s 2025 finding that “[t]he 
Confession of Judgment provisions of the . . . [guarantees] are valid and enforceable 
and WSFS is entitled to confess judgment against them.”  D.I. 27; Wilmington 
Savings Fund Society, FSB v. Wahl, 2025 WL 2206759 (Del. Super. Ct. Jul. 31, 2025) 
(Wahl I).  The Court recommitted the matter to that Commissioner to allow for the 
testimony of an additional witness.  D.I. 31.  After that witness t estified, the 
Commissioner again concluded “[t]he Confession of Judgment provisions of the . . 
. [guarantees] are valid and enforceable and WSFS is entitled to confess judgment 
against them.” D.I. 40; Wilmington Savings Fund Society, FSB v. Wahl , 2026 WL 
1747746 (Del. Super. Ct. June 16, 2026) (Wahl II).  Defendants again appealed.  D.I. 
41.  The parties agree that there is a single appeal before the Court.  D.I. 45.  This 
Order considers the facts developed at both evidentiary hearings in assessing the 
enforceability of the confession of judgment provisions.

the complete record in this matter, the Commissioner’s conclusion, finding “the 
confession of judgment provisions [to be] valid and enforceable against the 
Defendants,”3 is ADOPTED.

leads.text:
Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Segall 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06852 
 November 18, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., appellant, 
 v 
 Stephen L. Segall, etc., respondent, et al., defendants; Binay AYY, LLC, etc., nonparty-respondent. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on November 18, 2026 
 2024-04710, (Index No. 35642/18) 
 Betsy Barros, J.P. 
 Angela G. Iannacci 
 Donna-Marie E. Golia 
 Lisa S. Ottley, JJ. 

 Akerman LLP, New York, NY (Ashley S. Miller and Jordan M. Smith of counsel), for appellant. 
 Joseph J. Haspel, Middletown, NY, for respondents. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Rockland County (Keith J. Cornell, J.), dated January 31, 2024. The order, insofar as appealed from, upon renewal, in effect, vacated so much of an order of the same court (Thomas Zugibe, J.) dated October 20, 2022, as denied the prior cross-motion of the defendant Stephen L. Segall for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him and on his counterclaim to cancel and discharge of record the subject mortgage and, upon searching the record, awarded the plaintiff summary judgment dismissing that defendant's counterclaim, and thereupon granted that defendant's prior cross-motion. 
 ORDERED that the order dated January 31, 2024, is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs. 
 On December 8, 2006, Stephen L. Segall (hereinafter the defendant) and Wendy S. Segall (hereinafter together the borrowers) executed a note in the sum of $516,750 in favor of Option One Mortgage Corporation. The note was secured by a mortgage on certain real property located in New City. The borrowers executed a loan modification agreement dated October 1, 2008. The borrowers allegedly defaulted on their obligations under the note and mortgage by failing to make the monthly payments due March 1, 2009, and thereafter. 
 On June 10, 2009, the plaintiff, as the purported assignee of the mortgage, commenced an action (hereinafter the 2009 action) against the borrowers, among others, to foreclose the mortgage. The plaintiff elected in the complaint to call due the entire amount secured by the mortgage. 
 On December 24, 2010, the plaintiff commenced a second action (hereinafter the 2010 action) against the borrowers, among others, to foreclose the mortgage. 
 The plaintiff's motion to discontinue the 2009 action was granted in an order dated October 13, 2011. The plaintiff's motion to discontinue the 2010 action was granted in an order [*2] dated June 26, 2013. 
 On January 21, 2015, the plaintiff commenced a third action (hereinafter the 2015 action) against the borrowers, among others, to foreclose the mortgage. By deed dated July 27, 2015, the borrowers conveyed the property to the defendant only. In an order dated July 19, 2017, the Supreme Court, inter alia, granted the defendant's cross-motion to dismiss the complaint in the 2015 action insofar as asserted against him for failure to comply with RPAPL 1304. 
 On September 20, 2018, the plaintiff commenced this action against the borrowers, among others, to foreclose the mortgage. The defendant interposed an answer in which he asserted, among other things, an affirmative defense alleging that the action was barred by the statute of limitations and a counterclaim to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage. 
 In October 2019, the plaintiff moved, inter alia, for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant and for an order of reference. The defendant cross-moved for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him as barred by the statute of limitations and on his counterclaim to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage. 
 By deed dated December 17, 2019, the defendant conveyed the property to Binay AYY, LLC (hereinafter Binay). 
 In an order dated October 20, 2022, the Supreme Court denied the defendant's cross-motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him and on his counterclaim to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage on the ground that the 2009 and 2010 actions had been voluntarily discontinued, citing Freedom Mtge. Corp. v Engel ( 37 NY3d 1 , 29). Upon searching the record, the court awarded the plaintiff summary judgment dismissing the defendant's counterclaim. The court denied, with leave to renew, those branches of the plaintiff's motion which were for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant and for an order of reference. 
 In July 2023, the plaintiff moved, among other things, for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant, to strike the defendant's answer, and for an order of reference. Binay, as successor in interest to the defendant, and the defendant, cross-moved, inter alia, (1) pursuant to CPLR 1018 to substitute Binay in place of the defendant, and (2) for leave to renew the defendant's prior cross-motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him as barred by the statute of limitations and on his counterclaim to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage, based on a change in the law, arguing that the action was time-barred under the Foreclosure Abuse Prevention Act (FAPA) (L 2022, ch 821 [eff Dec. 30, 2022]). In an order dated January 31, 2024, the Supreme Court, among other things, denied the plaintiff's motion, denied, as academic, that branch of the cross-motion of Binay and the defendant which was to amend the caption to substitute Binay in the place of the defendant, granted that branch of the cross-motion which was for leave to renew, and, upon renewal, granted the defendant's prior cross-motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him as barred by the statute of limitations and on his counterclaim to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage. The plaintiff appeals from so much of the order as, upon renewal, granted the defendant's prior cross-motion. 
 "Pursuant to CPLR 1018, [u]pon any transfer of interest, the action may be continued by or against the original parties unless the court directs the person to whom the interest is transferred to be substituted or joined in the action" ( Wells Fargo Bank, NA v McKenzie , 183 AD3d 574, 575 [internal quotation marks omitted]). Thus, the defendant, as well as Binay, as the current owner of the premises and the successor in interest to the defendant, could defend the action in the absence of formal substitution or joinder ( see CPLR 1018; HSBC Bank USA, N.A. v Welt , 243 AD3d 770 , 771). 
 "An action to foreclose a mortgage is governed by a six-year statute of limitations" ( U.S. Bank N.A. v Santos , 218 AD3d 827, 828 ; see CPLR 213[4]). "[E]ven if a mortgage is payable in installments, once a mortgage debt is accelerated, the entire amount is due and the statute of limitations begins to run on the entire debt" ( Bank of N.Y. Mellon v Mor , 201 AD3d 691, 694 ). "The entire mortgage debt will be deemed to have been accelerated by, as relevant here, the commencement of a mortgage foreclosure action in which the complaint seeks payment of the full outstanding loan balance" ( U.S. Bank N.A. v Connor , 204 AD3d 861, 863 ). 
 "Pursuant to RPAPL 1501(4), a person having an estate or interest in real property subject to a mortgage may maintain an action to secure the cancellation and discharge of the encumbrance, and to adjudge the estate or interest free of it, if the applicable statute of limitations for commencing a foreclosure action has expired" ( U.S. Bank NA v Schaer , 223 AD3d 928 , 929). Here, in support of their cross-motion, Binay and the defendant established, prima facie, that the six-year statute of limitations began to run in June 2009, when the plaintiff commenced the 2009 action and elected in the complaint to call due the entire amount secured by the mortgage ( see Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v DiGiorgio , 237 AD3d 899 , 900). Since the plaintiff did not commence the instant action until September 2018, more than six years later, Binay and the defendant established, prima facie, that the action was time-barred ( see CPLR 213[4]; US Bank Trust, N.A. v Reizes , 222 AD3d 907, 910 ). 
 In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact. Pursuant to CPLR 3217, as amended by FAPA, the voluntary discontinuances of the 2009 and 2010 actions did not serve to revive or reset the statute of limitations ( see id. § 3217[e]; JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. v Turkov , 242 AD3d 1069 , 1071; Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Edwards , 231 AD3d 1189 , 1193). Moreover, as neither the 2009 action nor the 2010 action was dismissed "based on an expressed judicial determination, made upon a timely interposed defense, that the instrument was not validly accelerated" (CPLR 213[4][a]), the plaintiff is estopped from asserting that the debt was not validly accelerated by the commencement of either of those actions ( see CV XXVIII, LLC v Williams , 236 AD3d 753 , 755; US Bank Trust, N.A. v Reizes , 222 AD3d at 910 ). 
 There is no merit to the plaintiff's contention that FAPA does not apply retroactively ( see Van Dyke v U.S. Bank, N.A. , 45 NY3d 461 ; Article 13 LLC v Ponce De Leon Fed. Bank , 45 NY3d 441 ). The plaintiff's challenges to the constitutionality of the retroactive application of FAPA are also without merit ( see Van Dyke v U.S. Bank, N.A. , 45 NY3d 461 ; Article 13 LLC v Ponce De Leon Fed. Bank , 45 NY3d 441 ; FV-1, Inc. v Palaguachi , 234 AD3d 818 , 822; Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Dagrin , 233 AD3d 1065 , 1069-1071; 97 Lyman Ave., LLC v MTGLQ Invs., L.P. , 233 AD3d 1038 , 1043). 
 The plaintiff's contention that the action was timely commenced pursuant to either CPLR 205(a) or 205-a is improperly raised for the first time in its reply brief ( see Bank of Am., N.A. v McKeon , 241 AD3d 617 , 619). 
 The plaintiff's remaining contention is without merit. 
 Accordingly, the Supreme Court, upon renewal, properly granted the defendant's prior cross-motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him as barred by the statute of limitations and on his counterclaim to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage. 
 BARROS, J.P., IANNACCI, GOLIA and OTTLEY, JJ., concur. 
 ENTER: 
 Darrell M. Joseph 
 Clerk of the Court

Before:  M. J. KELLY, P.J., and RIORDAN and RICK, JJ. 
 
PER CURIAM. 
 This contract dispute involves a complaint filed by plaintiff Demmak Industries, LLC, 
d/b/a Iridium Manufacturing (“Iridium”), against defendant JAC Products, Inc.  (“JAC”), as well 
as a counterclaim filed by JAC against Iridium. The trial court dismissed Iridium’s complaint under 
MCR 2.116(C)(8) and (C)(10), and granted summary disposition in favor of JAC on its 
counterclaim under MCR 2.116(I)(2). Iridium appeals that order as of right, arguing that the trial 
court erred in its contractual analysis and that Iridium, not JAC, should prevail in this case because 
JAC materially breached the parties’ two related contracts. For the reasons set forth, we affirm the 
trial court in part, reverse in part, and remand to that court for further proceedings. 
I.  FACTS 
 JAC is an automotive-component supplier to companies such as Toyota and Stellantis, and 
Iridium is an automotive-parts manufacturer that contracts with suppliers such as JAC.1 On March 
19, 2019, JAC sent Iridium a letter informing Iridium of the following: 
 
 
1 While not clearly explained in the record, this relationship implies that JAC is a “Tier One” 
automotive supplier, i.e., a supplier directly to the original equipment manufacturer, and Iridium 
is a “Tier Two” automotive supplier, i.e., a supplier to Tier One.   
-2- 
 This letter is to inform you that JAC Products, Inc. (JAC) has awarded 
Iridium Manufacturing with the Toyota Tonneau program per the terms and 
conditions detailed below and subject to JAC Products’ standard purchase order 
terms and conditions (available on www.jacproducts.com). . . . 
The letter continued that JAC would supply certain basic materials to Iridium and, in turn, Iridium 
would manufacture the automotive parts required by JAC on a rolling basis: 
 Subject to the JAC Products purchase orders and standard purchase order 
terms and conditions, Iridium Manufacturing will supply to JAC Products 100% of 
JAC Products’ requirements for all products covered by this award letter for the 
production life of the Toyota Tonneau program at the pricing indicated in this award 
letter. 
* * * 
 JAC will provide and deliver all aluminum extrusions for use in production 
of all parts to be supplied by Iridium, for no cost to Iridium FOB at Iridium’s 
address in Sterling Heights, Michigan. 
The letter estimated that JAC would require 31,496 units for 2019, 28,585 units for 2020, and 
20,053 units for 2021. It was signed by a representative for Iridium the following day.2 
 On July 22, 2022, JAC sent Iridium another letter3 informing Iridium of the following: 
 This letter is to inform you that JAC Products, Inc. (JAC) has awarded 
Iridium Manufacturing with the Stellantis DS program as detailed below and 
subject to JAC Products’ standard purchase order terms and conditions (available 
on www.jacproducts.com). . . . 
The letter further provided: 
 Subject to the JAC Products purchase orders and standard purchase order 
terms and conditions, Iridium Manufacturing will supply to JAC Products 100% of 
JAC Products’ requirements for all products covered by this award letter for the 
production life of the Toyota Tonneau [sic: Stellantis DS ] program at the pricing 
indicated in this award letter in accordance with the firm quantities and delivery 
schedules specific in the JAC Products’ releases. 
* * * 
 
 
2 We hereinafter refer to this letter as the “Toyota Contract.”

the July 2022 letter was intended to supersede and replace that earlier letter.

 Weekly volume for Stellantis DS accounting for all parts will range from 
2,200pcs a week min to 3,600pcs a week max. 
The letter was signed by Iridium’s representative the following day.4

following relevant provisions:

apportionable under generally accepted accounting principles to the terminated 
portion of this Purchase Order. The foregoing amounts shall be Seller’s sole and 
exclusive recovery from Buyer (without regard to the legal theory which is the basis 
for any claim by Seller) on account of such termination. . . . Except as provided in 
this Paragraph, Buyer shall not be liable for and shall not be required to make 
payments to Seller, directly or on account of claims by Seller’s subcontractors, for 
loss of anticipated profit, unabsorbed overhead, interest on claims, product 
development and engineering costs, facilities and equipment rearrangement costs 
or rental, unamortized depreciation costs, general and administrative burden 
charges and other consequential or incidental damages from termination of this 
Purchase Order. . . . 
In August 2023, Iridium filed its complaint against JAC, alleging that “JAC has an 
outstanding balance of $428,252.10. This entire amount is for products that Iridium has already 
delivered to JAC.” Thus, Iridium maintained three claims against JAC: Count I  (breach of 
contract), Count II (unjust enrichment), and Count III (statutory conversion). 
 The following month, JAC filed a counterclaim against Iridium, alleging that “[d]uring the 
course of the contractual relationship between Iridium and JAC, Iridium repeatedly failed to 
provide timely delivery of quality parts” and that it had suffered damages in the approximate 
amount of $130,000. 
 In June 2025, JAC moved for summary disposition of Iridium’s complaint pursuant to 
MCR 2.116(C)(8) and (C)(10). In its accompanying brief, JAC explained additional details of the 
parties’ relationship. According to JAC, Iridium had deficient facilities and equipment, resulting 
in several issues such as a “busted door on Mill #1” and “down waterjets” in November 2022.  
JAC attempted to assist Iridium with production stability by, for example, providing Iridium with 
equipment and shifting some orders to another supplier with open capacity to reduce Iridium’s 
backlog.5 Unfortunately, these attempts were unsuccessful, and  in April 2023,  JAC invoked its 
right under ¶ 16 of the Purchase Order Terms and Conditions to terminate the parties’ contractual 
relationship. The April 2023 termination e-mail from JAC to Iridium stated, in relevant part: 
 Also, in order to recover the significant costs that JAC Products was forced 
to absorb since Iridium was not able to meet its obligated volumes, we are attaching 
an overview of these costs that JAC intends to short pay Iridium as a final matter 
of business and recover these costs.  
 A summary of these costs is as follows:  
 
 
5 JAC acknowledged that at one point during the parties’ relationship, JAC failed to timely deliver 
raw material to Iridium for a few months. However, JAC explained, it never sought to hold Iridium 
financially responsible for Iridium’s resulting late delivery. 
-5- 
 1. Iridium OT Charges - $28,000. This was the OT that JAC paid to Iridium 
to work weekends, and was not recovered from our customer.  
 2. Outside Processing Break in Charges - $60,000. This was $2,500 per 
occurrence from our coating supplier to break in to run the parts that Iridium was 
behind on, in order meet our customer requirements.  
 3. Premium Freight Due to Iridium capacity shortfall - 989 Hinges - 
$27,930. Expedites within our supply chain to prevent customer shutdowns for 
Toyota  
 4. Premium Freight Due to Iridium capacity shortfall - $15,000. Expedites 
within our supply chain to prevent customer shutdowns for Stellantis  
 Total - $130,930 
Iridium responded to the April 2023 termination e-mail a few weeks later, stating:6 
 I am writing to respond to your email of April 11. I dispute that Iridium 
“was not able to meet its obligated volumes” as you write in your email. In fact, it 
is JAC that did not perform under the agreements. After review of the material that 
I have on the floor, and an account of my records, the following payments are owed 
by JAC and are to be corrected.  
 Amounts owed to Iridium:

December 2022, incurred to help get JAC caught up on its releases, which

leads.caseName: Northern Biomedical Research Inc v. Nbr Investment Properties LLC
leads.text:
If this opinion indicates that it is “FOR PUBLICATION,” it is subject to 
revision until final publication in the Michigan Appeals Reports. 
 
 
 
 
-1- 
S T A T E  O F  M I C H I G A N  
 
C O U R T  O F  A P P E A L S  
 
 
 
NORTHERN BIOMEDICAL RESEARCH, INC. 
and 1210 PONTALUNA, LLC, 
 
 Plaintiffs/Counterdefendants-
Appellees/Cross-Appellants, 
 
 
UNPUBLISHED 
November 18, 2026 
11:34 AM 
v No. 369662 
Muskegon Circuit Court 
NBR INVESTMENT PROPERTIES, LLC, 
 
LC No. 2021-004490-CB 
 Defendant/Counterplaintiff-
Appellant/Cross-Appellee. 
 
 
 
Before:  SWARTZLE, P.J., and ACKERMAN and TREBILCOCK, JJ. 
 
PER CURIAM. 
 This case involves a lease between Northern Biomedical Research, Inc. and NBR 
Investment Properties, LLC (the Landlord).  The dispute between the parties arose when Northern 
Biomedical exercised the option under the lease to buy the property and received a n appraisal to 
determine the purchase price in accordance with the lease.  Once Landlord learned of the appraised 
value, it refused to sell the property to Northern Biomedical.  Northern Biomedical sued to 
complete the purchase, and Landlord countersued.  Northern Biomedical moved for summary 
disposition on liability, which the trial court granted in Northern Biomedic al’s favor.  Landlord 
now appeals, claiming errors with the trial court’s grant of summary disposition and specific 
performance.  Northern Biomedical filed a cross -appeal, arguing that the trial court erred when 
calculating damages and costs.  Finding no reversible error, we affirm.   
I. BACKGROUND 
 
-2- 
 Founded in 1996, Northern Biomedical is a non-clinical research company for drugs, cell 
therapy, and medical devices; Landlord owned the property that Northern Biomedical used 
including a laboratory.1  Robert Boyd was the principal owner of both entities.   
In 2019, BHJW Biomedical Research Corporation showed interest in purchasing Northern 
Biomedical and bought Northern Biomedical’s name and assets, thus becoming Northern 
Biomedical.  At the time, BHJW could not afford to buy the company and the property, so Landlord 
leased 65,000 square feet of the real property to the newly-acquired Northern Biomedical.  
 In the lease agreement, Northern Biomedical obtained an option to purchase the real 
property from Landlord during the lease term:  
22.1. Landlord grants to the Tenant an option to purchase the Property, which 
shall not be severable from the remaining terms and conditions of this Lease and 
shall not survive the expiration or earlier termination of this Lease.  The option to 
purchase shall be exercisable by written notice from Tenant to Landlord give [sic] 
at any time during the Lease term when the Lease is not in default.  
22.2. The purchase price shall be determined by appraisal conducted by a 
qualified appraiser mutually acceptable to Landlord and Tenant, the cost of which 
appraisal shall be born equally by the parties.  In the event Landlord and Tenant are 
unable to agree upon a qualified appraiser, each party shall select one qualified 
appraiser and the 2 qualified appraisers so selected shall choose a third qualified 
appraiser who will conduct the appraisal.  The purchase price [sic] payable by wire 
transfer of collected funds at the closing.   
Although the lease did not provide an exhaustive definition of “default,” the lease included 
the following provision pertaining to events of default: 
18. EVENTS OF DEFAULT.  Each of the following will constitute a default 
by Tenant under this Lease: (a) if Tenant fails to pay Rent or any other payment 
when due hereunder within five (5) days after written notice from Landlord of such 
failure to pay on the due date; or (b) if Tenant fails, whether by action or inaction, 
to timely comply with, or satisfy, any of the other obligations imposed on Tenant 
under this Lease (other than the obligation to pay Rent) for a period of thirty (30) 
days after Landlord’s delivery to Tenant of written notice of such default under this 
Section 18; provided, however, that if the default cannot, by its nature, be cured 
within such thirty (30) day period, but Tenant commences and diligently pursues a 
cure of such default promptly within the initial thirty (30) day cure period, then 
Landlord will not exercise its remedies for so long as Tenant will have commenced 
cure within such thirty (30) days and will be diligently prosecuting the same to 
completion.   
 
 
1 Landlord originally owned real property and operated a biomedical research company on that 
property.   
 
-3- 
Pertinent here, the lease also provided the following provisions pertaining to assignment 
restrictions, Landlord’s maintenance, option to lease vacant portions of the property, waiver of 
consequential damages, and confidentiality: 
8. ASSIGNMENT AND SUBLETTING.  Tenant will not, without the prior 
written consent of Landlord, which consent may not unreasonably be withheld in 
Landlord’s sole discretion, (a) assign, pledge or mortgage this Lease or any interest 
hereunder; (b) permit any assignment hereof by operati on of law; (c) sublet the 
Premises or any part thereof; or (d) permit the use of the Premises by any party 
other than Tenant and its agents and business visitors. 
*   *   * 
12.3. Landlord shall, at its expense, keep and maintain all other portions of the 
Property, other than the Premises and the Common Areas, in a good and clean 
operating condition and in compliance with all applicable laws, ordinances and 
regulations. 
*   *   * 
19.3. Waiver of Consequential Punitive, Exemplary Damages.  Landlord and 
Tenant each hereby waive their right to seek to recover any consequential, punitive, 
or exemplary damages. 
*   *   * 
23.1. For purposes of this Lease, the term “Vacant Premises” shall mean all 
rentable portions of the Property, other than the Premises, that are vacant, and the 
term “Other Premises” shall mean all rentable portions of the Property, other than 
the Premises.  Dur ing the Term, Tenant shall have the option to lease the Vacant 
Premises or any portion thereof.   Tenant shall exercise this option, if at all, by 
submitting written notice of Tenant’s exercise of the option (“Option Notice”), 
which shall include a description of the Vacant Premises to be leased (“Expansion 
Premises”) and the date on which Tenant would like to add such Expansion 
Premises to the Premises (“Expansion Date”).  If Tenant exercises this option, the 
Expansion Premises shall become part of the Premises on the Expansion Date.  The 
rent per square foot of the Expansion Premises shall be the same as the rent per 
square foot of the Premises as of the Expansion Date.  Effective as of the Expansion 
Date, the Tenant’s Pro Rata Share shall be a fraction in which the numerator is the 
number of rentable square feet in the Premises including the Expansion Premises 
and the denominator is the total number of rentable square feet in the building on 
the Property. 
*   *   * 
24.6 Confidential Information.  Landlord and Tenant agree to maintain in strict 
confidence the economic terms of this Lease.   
 
-4- 
 On July 1, 2021, Northern Biomedical communicated its exercise of the option to purchase 
the property in a written letter: “In accordance with Section 22.1 of the Lease, Tenant hereby 
exercises its right to purchase all of Landlord’s right, title, and interest in and to th e Property on 
the terms and conditions provided in the Lease.”  The parties subsequently entered into an 
“Agreement Regarding Lease Option to Purchase,” which outlined that Northern Biomedical  
“exercised its option to purchase the Property,” established a closing date for sale of the property, 
and provided that the agreement was binding on the parties and their “permitted assigns.”   
To determine the purchase price, according to the option provision, an appraisal had to be 
done.  Northern Biomedical picked Stacey Broersma as its appraiser , and Landlord chose Jeff 
Genzink.  Because the parties could not agree on an appraiser, a third appraiser had to be chosen.  
Broersma and Genzink both suggested Doug Adams, and Genzink agreed to the selection.  
Broersma sent an e-mail to Adams that the appraisal was for “the Fee Simple Estate Market Value 
of the property, excluding the current lease agreements.”   
  Before the appraisal was conducted, Northern Biomedical’s counsel sent an e -mail to 
Landlord’s counsel that it was considering assigning the option to 1210 Pontaluna, LLC (a 
company with members who were shareholders of Northern Biomedical) and sent a prop osed 
assignment document.  Landlord’s counsel told Northern Biomedical’s counsel that the 
“assignment look[ed] good” and requested an executed copy of the assignment.  When Northern 
Biomedical’s counsel sent closing documents several days before the target closing date, including 
the assignment of the purchase option, Landlord’s counsel stated it was going to “review the 
documents and get back to [Northern Biomedical] with any edits.”2  
The assignment from Northern Biomedical to 1210 Pontaluna was effective upon execution 
by each party; it was not made dependent on the prior consent of Landlord, though there was a 
signature page for Landlord to indicate its consent (this went unsigned).  The assignment did 
include a proviso that Northern Biomedical remained committed to the purchase of the property 
“in the event that” 1210 Pontaluna “fails to do so.”  The proviso was added at the request of 
Landlord: “we would be comfortable with the tenant assigning its right under the agreement 
pursuant to a written assignment which specifically states that the tenant is not relieved of its 
obligation to purchase the property.”   
 Adams submitted his appraisal.  The appraisal outlined that the best use of the property 
was a warehouse because the demand for a life -science laboratory in the area was low.  Because 
of this, the property’s value was reduced by $1.1 million as an estimate d cost of removing the 
laboratory.  With that adjustment, the net appraised value was $8.87 million.  Landlord conveyed 
its dissatisfaction with the appraisal to Northern Biomedical and requested an extension to the 
closing date to obtain a separate appraisal.  Northern Biomedical refused to grant the extension , 
and Landlord refused to close the sale.   
 
 
2 Boyd testified that he had concerns that the option paperwork list ed Northern Biomedical as a 
Michigan corporation when it had reincorporated as a Delaware corporation.  Landlord mentions 
this in its brief as support that Boyd did not approve of the assignment.   
 
-5- 
 Because of Landlord’s refusal to close the sale, Northern Biomedical sued Landlord 
claiming in part breaches of the lease and option and seeking specific performance as well as 
monetary damages.  Landlord counterclaimed, requesting declaratory relief regar ding the option, 
appraisal, and purchase price, as well as breach of lease.  Landlord claimed that Northern 
Biomedical materially breached the lease by assigning the option without consent, failing to 
disclose the appraisers’ conflict of interest, being late in paying rent, u sing more space in the 
property than was leased, and being delinquent in reimbursing property taxes.   
As the lawsuit ensued, Northern Biomedical sought to exercise the option to lease the 
vacant space.  Landlord responded, “Given Tenant’s multiple prior breaches of the lease as 
documented in our counterclaim, we cannot agree that the option [to lease vacan t space] remains 
available to [Tenant].  Instead, Landlord will consider entering into a separate lease with Tenant 
related to the additional office space.”  The parties negotiated terms to lease the vacant space, but 
Northern Biomedical eventually execute d a two-year lease at a separate, unrelated location  (570 
Seminole Road) at a higher rental rate .  Northern Biomedical amended its complaint to include a 
claim regarding the option to lease and
